old: China’s own party judged him 70% right, 30% wrong (1981).
new: China’s own party judged his merits primary and his errors secondary (1981), often summarized as 70% right, 30% wrong.
problem: The 1981 Resolution does not contain the 70/30 formula; it says Mao’s merits are primary and his errors secondary, and 70/30 is a later popular shorthand (associated with Deng).
sources: 1981 Resolution text, para. 27: “his merits are primary and his errors secondary”

old: The party’s Resolution on History: Mao 70% right, 30% wrong; the Cultural Revolution was a catastrophe.
new: The party’s Resolution on History: Mao’s merits primary, his errors secondary (popularly “70% right, 30% wrong”); the Cultural Revolution was a catastrophe.
problem: Attributes the 70/30 formula to the 1981 Resolution, which does not use it.

old: The 1981 Resolution and the 2021 Resolution both call it a serious error, though without a death toll.
new: The 1981 Resolution calls it a serious error and the 2021 Resolution lists it among the party’s mistakes, both without a death toll.
problem: The 2021 Resolution only says “mistakes were made such as the Great Leap Forward” and is notably softer than 1981’s “serious mistakes” language.

old: female genital cutting and forced marriage outlawed.
new: campaigns against female genital cutting and forced marriage (female genital cutting was made a crime only in 1996).
problem: Sankara’s government campaigned against these practices, but FGM was criminalized only by Law 43/96/ADP (1996, in force 1997), long after his death.

old: Cuban troops in Angola help defeat South African forces (Cuito Cuanavale, 1988).
new: Cuban troops in Angola fight South African forces; both sides claim victory at Cuito Cuanavale (1988), which is followed by talks on Namibian independence.
problem: States a contested outcome as settled: both Cuba/Angola and South Africa claim victory at Cuito Cuanavale, and historians still dispute it.

new: brings repeated island-wide blackouts (at least six by September).
problem: Out of date: Cuba had at least six nationwide grid collapses in 2026, the latest on September 18.

new: calling for urgent market reforms; on June 18 the National Assembly approves more than 175 of them. (developing)
problem: Omits that the reforms were actually adopted: the National Assembly unanimously approved a package of 175+ market measures on June 18, 2026.

old: The party is debating opening to private business on the China and Vietnam model.
new: In June the National Assembly approved more than 175 market reforms, including larger private firms and private banks, while leaders insist Cuba is not giving up socialism.
problem: Out of date: the opening is no longer just under debate; reforms allowing firms over 100 staff, private banks and sales of state property were approved in June 2026 and are being implemented.

old: China, Vietnam, Laos; Cuba is now debating it
new: China, Vietnam, Laos; Cuba began adopting parts of it in 2026
problem: Out of date: Cuba’s National Assembly approved a large market-reform package in June 2026.
Wrong date and missing co-author: Cuba’s Aborted Reform by Carmelo Mesa-Lago and Jorge Pérez-López was published by University Press of Florida in 2005.
sources: Cambridge Core review: Latin American Politics and Society, Mesa-Lago and Pérez-López, Cuba’s Aborted Reform (Gainesville: University Press of Florida, 2005)

new: now: 'Six UN-member successor states, plus Kosovo, whose independence Serbia does not recognize.'
problem: Counting Kosovo as a successor state without qualification states a contested sovereignty question as settled.
